key_points.point: AI experts hold a significantly more optimistic view of AI's long-term impact on the U.S. than the general public. They believe AI will drive substantial productivity gains and positive outcomes in sectors like the economy, healthcare, and education. This belief is grounded in the expert consensus that AI serves as a powerful tool for enhancing human capability and societal progress.
key_points.verbatim: Fully 56% of AI experts surveyed say AI will have a very or somewhat positive impact on the United States over the next 20 years. This compares with 17% among the general public.

key_points.point: Experts view AI as a tool that will enhance professional productivity and create new opportunities, contrasting with the public's anxiety regarding job displacement. This perspective emphasizes the role of AI as an expert's assistant that improves how work is performed.
key_points.verbatim: While 73% of AI experts surveyed say AI will have a very or somewhat positive impact on how people do their jobs over the next 20 years, that share drops to 23% among U.S. adults.

key_points.point: AI experts emphasize the utility of AI in automating repetitive and mundane tasks, viewing it as a tool to enhance efficiency and productivity. This aligns with the accelerationist focus on leveraging AI as a force for progress and labor optimization. The document highlights expert optimism regarding AI's potential to improve outcomes in specialized fields like medicine.
key_points.verbatim: I think broadly some of the things that excite me are things like applications that can save people a lot of time from repetitive and mundane tasks. So I think automating some of those workflows.

key_points.point: AI experts express significant optimism regarding AI's capacity to improve diagnostic accuracy and accelerate medical treatment development. This belief in AI's transformative power to solve complex, high-stakes problems like disease classification supports the accelerationist view of AI as a catalyst for human advancement.
key_points.verbatim: I’ve seen that the AI can improve a lot the accuracy of the diagnosis of different diseases. Also, it can boost the development of different medicines for different treatments.

key_points.point: Experts emphasize AI's role in automating slow, repetitive processes, thereby freeing up human capacity for higher-level work. This perspective frames AI as a catalyst for efficiency rather than a replacement for human intelligence, supporting the accelerationist view that AI supercharges human potential.
key_points.verbatim: In general, I think of AI as helping people along jobs. So, I think of the biggest outcome is automation of processes that feel very slow and feel like they don't necessarily require full brain power, being automated by AI.

key_points.point: AI experts demonstrate a high degree of optimism regarding the personal benefits of AI, with 76% stating that increased use is more likely to benefit them than harm them. This belief suggests that those closest to the technology's development perceive it as a net positive for their own professional and personal lives. The data indicates a strong consensus among experts that AI serves as a productive tool, contrasting with the more cautious or negative outlooks found in the general public. This aligns with the accelerationist view that AI is a revolutionary force for individual and societal advancement.
key_points.verbatim: Thinking about yourself, do you think the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI) is more likely to... Benefit you than harm you... 76% [AI experts]
key_points.excerpt_context: Page 82, Views of personal benefit versus harm from AI, among AI experts

key_points.point: Both the public and AI experts express a strong desire for increased government regulation of AI, with a shared concern that current oversight is insufficient. This indicates a consensus that the current regulatory environment is too lax to manage the risks associated with rapid AI development.
key_points.verbatim: Both the public and experts largely worry the U.S. government will not go far enough in regulating AI. About six-in-ten U.S. adults and 56% of experts surveyed say theyÆre more concerned about this than about the government going too far.

key_points.point: There is widespread skepticism regarding the ability of private companies to develop and deploy AI responsibly. A majority of both the public and experts lack confidence in industry efforts, suggesting that corporate self-regulation is viewed as inadequate.
key_points.verbatim: They are also largely skeptical of industry efforts around responsible AI: 59% of the public and 55% of surveyed experts have not too much or no confidence in U.S. companies to develop and use AI responsibly.

key_points.point: Experts and the public share deep concerns regarding the potential for AI to facilitate misinformation at scale and enable data misuse. This belief in the catastrophic potential of AI-driven information manipulation aligns with safetyist concerns about the societal risks of unaligned or uncontrolled systems.
key_points.verbatim: But I think the main issue with AI and misinformation is that you can now do misinformation at scale, at a way larger scale.

key_points.point: The general public expresses significant anxiety regarding AI's potential to cause major harm to humans and eliminate jobs. This skepticism contrasts sharply with the expert community's more optimistic outlook, highlighting a fundamental disagreement on the risks posed by AI deployment.
key_points.verbatim: The belief that AI will cause major harm to humans is more common among the public than AI experts. U.S. adults are more likely than experts to believe AI will cause major harm to humans (35% vs. 20%).

key_points.point: There is a clear need for transparency and mechanisms for public recourse, such as opting out or correcting AI-generated representations. This reflects a safetyist intention to prioritize human agency and accountability in the face of rapid AI integration.
key_points.verbatim: Companies need to be transparent, and they need to include ways for people to either opt out or to correct anything that does not represent a person in their product.

key_points.point: The research methodology emphasizes the inclusion of diverse perspectives in AI governance and design, specifically by consulting an advisory board with expertise in ethics and bias. This aligns with safetyist intentions to ensure that AI development is guided by rigorous, multi-disciplinary oversight. The inclusion of conferences like FAccT and AIES in the sampling frame further demonstrates a commitment to prioritizing ethical and social science implications in AI research.
key_points.verbatim: This board included experts in a variety of areas related to artificial intelligence, including computer science, ethics, biases and other areas.

key_points.point: There is a significant gap between the public and AI experts regarding the perceived risks of AI, particularly concerning the potential for major harm. While experts are generally more optimistic about personal benefits, they still acknowledge the potential for catastrophic outcomes, with 35% of experts believing it is 'extremely' or 'very' likely that AI will cause major harm to humans in the next 20 years. This reflects a safetyist concern that even those building the technology recognize existential or major societal risks. The data highlights a persistent anxiety about the trajectory of AI development despite the perceived productivity gains.
key_points.verbatim: Thinking about the next 20 years, how likely do you think it is that artificial intelligence (AI) will... Cause major harm to humans... 6% Extremely likely, 14% Very likely [AI experts]

key_points.point: The general public exhibits significant anxiety regarding AI-driven labor displacement, with a majority believing that AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years. This reflects a deep-seated concern about the economic impact of automation on the workforce.
key_points.verbatim: Throughout our prior work, the public has been wary about AIÆs role in job loss. In our current survey, 64% of the public thinks AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next 20 years.

key_points.point: Both experts and the public are highly concerned about bias in AI decision-making, highlighting the potential for algorithmic systems to perpetuate or exacerbate existing societal inequalities.
key_points.verbatim: Bias in decisions made by AI is also a concern for experts and the public (55% each say theyÆre highly concerned).

key_points.point: Experts working in non-profit sectors express a desire for a balanced approach that allows for innovation while simultaneously demanding guardrails. This reflects the skeptic's strategy of maintaining critical vigilance while acknowledging potential benefits.
key_points.verbatim: So I’m on both sides of this. I think we need to have limited regulations so that we can innovate and we can compete, because if we regulate too much, we’re going to be left behind — [but] for us not to have guardrails around [AI], to me, is wild.

key_points.point: The document identifies a widespread lack of confidence in both the government's ability to regulate AI and corporations' willingness to develop it responsibly. This skepticism regarding institutional competence is a core component of the skeptic's critique of current AI governance.
key_points.verbatim: There’s little confidence in the government to regulate AI effectively: 62% of the public and 53% of AI experts surveyed have not too much or no confidence in the U.S. government to regulate AI effectively.

key_points.point: Both the public and experts acknowledge that AI will lead to fewer jobs in specific sectors like trucking, journalism, and manufacturing. This consensus validates the skeptic concern regarding the disruptive and potentially negative impact of AI on the workforce.
key_points.verbatim: Overall, 64% of U.S. adults say that over the next 20 years, AI will lead to fewer jobs in the U.S., while just 5% think it will lead to more jobs.

key_points.point: There is widespread concern among both the public and experts regarding AI's negative impact on elections and journalism. This shared wariness suggests that AI is viewed as a threat to democratic processes and the integrity of information, aligning with skeptic concerns about institutional erosion.
key_points.verbatim: AI experts and the public are both wary of AIÆs role in politics and journalism. Just 11% of experts surveyed and 9% of the public believe AI will positively impact elections in the U.S. over the next 20 years.

key_points.point: The document highlights a significant concern among AI experts regarding the lack of representation of Black and Hispanic perspectives in AI design. A majority of experts (52%) believe these groups are not well represented, which supports the skeptic desire to identify and eliminate structural biases in AI development. This finding underscores the need for more inclusive design processes to prevent the perpetuation of historical prejudices.
key_points.verbatim: 52% of AI experts who say they who think the people who design artificial intelligence (AI) computer programs take into account the experiences and views of Black adults Not too/ Not at all well.

key_points.point: The study employs a rigorous, multi-conference sampling strategy to capture a wide range of perspectives on AI, including those focused on fairness and ethics. By systematically surveying experts from conferences like FAccT and EAAMO, the researchers intend to create a representative baseline of expert opinion on bias and societal impact. This approach facilitates the systematic evaluation of how the AI community perceives its own role in addressing social harms.
key_points.verbatim: The list was developed in consultation with external advisers on the project (refer to the end of this methodology) and was designed to capture as diverse and wide a range of perspectives on AI as possible.

key_points.point: The survey data reveals a widespread public perception that AI designers fail to account for the experiences and views of women. Only 27% of U.S. adults believe designers take these views into account 'very' or 'somewhat' well, while 35% believe they do not. This empirical evidence of public distrust suggests a perceived structural bias in the AI development lifecycle. Skeptics use this data to argue that the current AI development process is exclusionary and fails to represent diverse societal perspectives.
key_points.verbatim: How representation of women's perspectives in AI design is viewed, among the U.S. public... Very/Somewhat well 27%, Not too/Not at all well 35%
key_points.excerpt_context: Page 81, How representation of women's perspectives in AI design is viewed, among the U.S. public

key_points.point: Public opinion strongly leans toward the belief that AI will lead to fewer jobs rather than more, with 64% of U.S. adults predicting a net decrease in employment over the next 20 years. This belief is particularly pronounced regarding roles like cashiers and factory workers, where the public expects significant displacement. This skepticism regarding the economic benefits of AI reflects a deep-seated concern about labor market stability and the potential for AI to exacerbate economic inequality.
key_points.verbatim: Thinking about the U.S. over the next 20 years, do you think that artificial intelligence (AI) will lead to... Fewer jobs... 64% [U.S. adults]
